Reviewer #2:

How root feeding insects orient in the soil towards their host plants and the contribution of root-associated CO2 as well as other root-derived chemical stimuli to this process is still a matter of debate and in many aspects an open research question. In this study Arce et al. identify among three candidates one molecular receptor for CO2 perception in larvae of the western corn root worm (WCR). Through a series of behavioural experiments employing the RNAi knockdown technique they demonstrate that this single receptor is both essential and sufficient to mediate behavioural responses to CO2 in a dose dependent manner from attraction to repellence form low to high CO2 concentrations, respectively. Further experiments show that, while other root derived stimuli attract WCR larvae on a short range irrespective of the CO2 receptor being silenced or not, CO2 unfolds its behavioural activity over longer distances. The authors also demonstrate that maize roots establish CO2 gradients in the soil with steeper gradients around highly fertilised plants, while WCR larvae grow better when feeding on the latter. By showing that WCR larvae move towards the source in all CO2 gradients encountered under field-relevant conditions, they discuss an enhanced probability for well-nourished maize plants, which emit more CO2 compared to plants under a poor fertiliser regime, to be found by one of their major insect herbivores.

Strengths

The manuscript is very well written and gives an excellent overview on the state of the art as introduction. The combination of molecular techniques and behavioural experiments provides novel and unique insights into the orientation of a root feeding insect below ground and the role of CO2 as an important cue in host location over long distances compared to other root-derived volatiles. By using the RNAi technique the authors reliably demonstrate that the targeted CO2 receptor is not required for the insect to respond to other cues, be they volatile or soluble compounds like sugars. The multitude of experimental techniques is well documented. The Discussion highlights as a striking difference to other species that a single molecular receptor mediates the full range of behavioural responses to CO2. It also carefully addresses different aspects and stages of host location from random walk with no available cue to upward orientation within a CO2 gradient at longer distances while other root-derived volatiles gain behavioural relevance at shorter distances even whit a silenced CO2 receptor. In summary these results are noteworthy with respect to the notorious difficulties of assessing insect behaviour below ground.

Weaknesses

By applying a number of different behavioural experiments including volatile and non-volatile stimuli in settings with and without substrate the authors have to some extend limited the informative value of their otherwise excellent and comprehensive work. Responses to volatile and non-volatile stimuli not only involve different sensory modalities, but also different physical processes below ground. While volatile stimuli may – depending on their valence – serve as attractants or repellents, non-volatile stimuli, which are applied at a single point in an arena with no established concentration gradient, may only arrest insects upon contact. Consequently, the latter stimuli contribute little if anything to the authors quest of understanding how host plants are not only located but also assessed from a distance through sensing of CO2 and interacting volatile stimuli. This interaction aspect is of special interest since, as stressed by the authors themselves, CO2 is emitted by almost every respiring soil organism and therefore a cue of limited reliability.

Abstract – please reword to: „…is specifically required for dose-dependent responses.… but silencing does not impair responses to other cues, search behaviour or motility". Rationale: This is what your impressing set of experiments has shown. Still, whether CO2 “influences" responses to some chemical stimuli or vice versa remains another question. E.g., how would it interact with methyl anthranilate etc.

Abstract: add “cue” after location

Results: Please reword; unless a gradient of non-volatile cues like sugars or DIMBOA is comprehensibly established in the substrate these cues should not be coined „attractants". In your experiment these cues are exposed to the larvae on a piece of filter paper on a moist substrate. That means no or neglectable diffusion into the substrate. Obviously, these compounds arrest the larvae upon contact, while the control stimulus does not. Please also check the rest of the manuscript with respect to this issue.

Results and Figure 3: Changing the sequence within the Figure would help readers to quickly grasp that (D), (E), and (F) have been performed in the petri-dish experiment instead of the olfactometer. Please place the petri dish at position D, D to E, E to F etc.

Results: place „(D)" before ‚Mean…' to consistently introduce to the different parts of the figure/caption as with (A), (B) etc.

Figure 6: Negative values on the x-axis have shadowy white squares in-between. Please remove for the print version.

Materials and methods: To the best of my knowledge, a conventional FID does not detect CO2. However, with some adaptation of the instrument, e.g. a methaniser chamber located between the column outlet and the FID, CO2 detection and quantitation becomes feasible. Please provide respective info and very briefly outline how the instrument has been calibrated. Otherwise readers my wonder.…

Materials and methods: were instead of „where" and suggestion for rewording:.… were found at a distance of 1 cm or less from the.…

Legend to Figure S1F: Check assignment; it doesn't seem to fit to Figure 6 of the main text.

results.result: Maize plants create CO2 gradients in soil, with concentrations decreasing from 548-554 ppm in the rhizosphere to 425-439 ppm at distances >40 cm. These gradients disappear when plants are removed, and CO2 measured around washed roots accounts for the difference between planted and unplanted soil.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide converging evidence from spatial CO2 measurements (C1, C2), control experiments without plants (C3), and measurements around isolated roots (C4). The data demonstrate that maize roots are the source of elevated soil CO2. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3) and appropriate controls are included.

results.result: The WCR genome encodes three putative CO2 receptors (DvvGr1, DvvGr2, DvvGr3) with seven transmembrane domains consistent with receptor topology. DvvGr1 and DvvGr2 show significantly higher expression in larval heads compared to bodies, while DvvGr3 shows no tissue-specific expression difference.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 and C53 are supported by genomic analysis, phylogenetic reconstruction, gene expression measurements (n=10), and protein structure predictions. The tissue-specific expression patterns for DvvGr1 and DvvGr2 are statistically significant, and the seven-transmembrane domain structure is consistent with known receptor proteins.

results.result: RNAi-mediated silencing of DvvGr2 (83% reduction) eliminates larval preference for elevated CO2, while silencing DvvGr1 or DvvGr3 (80% and 66% reduction respectively) does not affect CO2 preference. Only DvvGr2 is crucial for CO2 responsiveness in WCR larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C11-C13, and C59 demonstrate specific requirement for DvvGr2 through gene-specific RNAi knockdown and behavioral assays. The differential effects of silencing the three receptors provide strong evidence for DvvGr2's unique role. Sample sizes (n=7 olfactometers) and controls (GFP dsRNA) are appropriate.

results.result: DvvGr2 silencing specifically eliminates CO2 responsiveness without affecting responses to other chemical cues including methyl anthranilate, Fe(III)(DIMBOA)3, or sugars, demonstrating that the behavioral phenotype is specific to CO2 perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C15, C54, and C80 provide multiple lines of evidence showing retained responses to volatile (methyl anthranilate) and non-volatile (Fe(III)(DIMBOA)3, sugars) compounds in DvvGr2-silenced larvae. This specificity control is critical for ruling out general sensory or behavioral defects. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-20).

results.result: Wild-type larvae show dose-dependent behavioral responses to CO2, with attraction at 59-258 ppm above ambient and repulsion at ≥950 ppm above ambient. DvvGr2-silenced larvae show no response at any tested concentration, demonstrating that DvvGr2 is specifically required for dose-dependent CO2 responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 and C115 demonstrate dose-response relationships in wild-type larvae and complete loss of CO2 responsiveness in DvvGr2-silenced larvae across the entire concentration range tested. The dose-response data are comprehensive and the loss-of-function phenotype is complete. Sample size (n=3) is modest but consistent effects are observed.

results.result: DvvGr2-silenced larvae exhibit normal motility and turning behavior but fail to orient toward CO2 point sources. However, both wild-type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae locate maize roots at short distances (<9 cm) with similar speed and efficiency, indicating that DvvGr2 is required for CO2 detection but not for short-range host location or general motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C25 use trajectory tracking to demonstrate that DvvGr2 silencing specifically impairs CO2-directed movement without affecting general locomotion or short-range host location. The distinction between CO2-dependent and CO2-independent host location is well-supported by comparing behavior with synthetic CO2 sources versus actual roots. Sample size (n=6) is adequate for behavioral tracking.

results.result: At 9 cm distance, both wild-type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae locate host plants even when CO2 is scrubbed with soda lime, indicating CO2-independent host location at short range. At 18 cm distance, wild-type larvae require CO2 for host location (eliminated by soda lime or DvvGr2 silencing), demonstrating distance-dependent reliance on CO2 for host location beyond 9 cm.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C34 and C113 provide strong evidence for distance-dependent host location mechanisms through systematic manipulation of distance (9 vs 18 cm), CO2 availability (soda lime scrubbing), and CO2 perception (DvvGr2 silencing). The soda lime validation showing no effect on other volatiles (C28) is critical. Sample sizes (n=4) are adequate and the pattern is consistent across manipulations.

results.result: In soil arenas, CO2 gradients extend to 32 cm from plants. DvvGr2-silenced larvae show impaired host location in a distance-dependent manner, with the largest differences at 64 cm (53% vs 33% reaching plants) and smallest at 16 cm. Time-course experiments show wild-type larvae reach plants faster (90% by 32h) than DvvGr2-silenced larvae (56% by 32h). Larvae released beyond the CO2 gradient (>32 cm) still locate plants in a DvvGr2-dependent manner, likely through random movement until encountering the gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C46, C68-C69 provide comprehensive evidence from soil arena experiments with multiple release distances (16-64 cm), time-course data, and CO2 gradient measurements. The distance-dependent effects are statistically significant and consistent with the measured CO2 gradient extent. Sample sizes are robust (n=6 trays with 20 larvae each). The interpretation of random movement beyond the gradient (C46, C70) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Well-fertilized plants emit higher CO2 levels than medium- or low-fertilized plants. Wild-type larvae preferentially locate well-fertilized plants at agriculturally relevant distances (~50 cm), while DvvGr2-silenced larvae show no preference. Larvae gain more weight on well-fertilized plants, demonstrating that CO2-mediated host selection has fitness consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52, C81, and C114 link plant nutritional status to CO2 emission, larval preference, and performance. The CO2 measurements, choice experiments (n=6), and performance assays (n=20) provide converging evidence that CO2 perception allows larvae to locate higher-quality hosts. The connection between preference and performance strengthens the adaptive interpretation.

results.result: CO2 receptor requirements vary across insect species: both Gr1 and Gr3 are required in Aedes aegypti, Helicoverpa armigera, and Drosophila melanogaster; both Gr2 and Gr3 are required in Culex quinquefasciatus (with Gr1 as modulator); and Gr2's role in Aedes aegypti is debated. This suggests species-specific molecular requirements for CO2 perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 accurately summarize prior literature on CO2 receptors across species. The citations support the stated findings, and the inference of species-specificity (C58) is reasonable given the variation. However, this is primarily a literature review result rather than new experimental data.

results.result: The roles of DvvGr1 and DvvGr3 remain undetermined, but their presence and expression may indicate additional complexity in developmental or tissue-specific CO2 responsiveness patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is speculative, acknowledging that the function of DvvGr1 and DvvGr3 is unknown. While their expression is documented (C6, C7), no functional role was demonstrated in the tested conditions. The speculation about developmental or tissue-specific roles is reasonable but unsupported by data.

results.result: Previous studies have identified multiple volatile cues affecting WCR larvae: (E)-β-caryophyllene attracts second and third instar larvae, ethylene attracts larvae, MBOA has been proposed as an attractant, and methyl anthranilate repels larvae. Many other herbivores respond to plant volatiles besides CO2.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 accurately cite prior literature on WCR responses to various volatiles. These are well-established findings from previous studies and provide important context for the current work. This is a literature review result.

results.result: Integration of multiple volatile cues allows WCR larvae to locate maize plants even without reliable CO2 gradients, increasing foraging robustness at short distances. CO2 may not play a role as a cue at close range, while other volatiles are more important at short than long distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C66, C67, and C92 are supported by the experimental data showing CO2-independent host location at short distances (C29-C30) and distance-dependent effects of CO2 removal (C31-C33). The inference that multiple cues increase robustness is reasonable and consistent with the data.

results.result: Larvae released beyond the CO2 gradient (>32 cm) may locate plants through random movement until encountering the gradient, or through localized CO2 gradients along preferential gas-phase pathways extending beyond 32 cm, or a combination of both. Random movement may help larvae find host cues at greater distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C70 and C93 are speculative explanations for how larvae locate plants from distances beyond the measured CO2 gradient. While the speculation is reasonable, no direct evidence is provided for random movement patterns or preferential gas-phase pathways. The data show DvvGr2-dependent location from >32 cm (C69) but don't distinguish between proposed mechanisms.

results.result: CO2 is abundantly produced, relatively stable, and diffuses rapidly in air, water, and soil, making it suitable for locating organisms with high respiratory rates. Aboveground insects can detect CO2 at 10-60 m, while belowground insects are hypothesized to detect it within the lower centimeter range due to reduced soil diffusion. Other volatiles like (E)-β-caryophyllene are unlikely detectable beyond 10 cm in soil.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 accurately cite prior literature on CO2 properties and detection distances. The comparison between aboveground and belowground detection distances is well-supported by citations. The inference about (E)-β-caryophyllene detection limits (C75-C76) is supported by cited studies on volatile diffusion in soil.

results.result: WCR's integration of CO2 with other environmental cues and context-dependent CO2 attraction parallels patterns in mosquitoes and hawkmoths. In Drosophila, CO2 receptors are involved in detecting other volatiles, with Gr63a required for short-term (<1 min) but not long-term (hours) spermidine attraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 accurately cite prior literature and make reasonable comparisons between WCR and other insect systems. The comparison strengthens the interpretation of WCR results by placing them in a broader context. However, these are primarily literature-based contextual claims.

results.result: WCR larvae are resistant to maize defenses and specialized on maize in agricultural monocultures. Well-fertilized plants increase photosynthesis and CO2 release. Following the strongest CO2 gradient may be adaptive for WCR, allowing location of not just any maize plant but specifically vigorous, high-quality hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C84, and C85 cite prior literature on WCR biology and plant physiology. Claims C83 and C86 make reasonable adaptive inferences based on the experimental data (C47-C51) showing preference for and better performance on well-fertilized plants. However, the adaptive interpretation is somewhat speculative as it wasn't directly tested whether larvae actually choose between multiple CO2 gradients.

results.result: CO2 emission correlates with resource profitability in multiple systems: Datura flowers emit highest CO2 when nectar is abundant (attracting hawkmoths), and apple lesions emit high CO2 (attracting fruit flies). This supports the hypothesis that CO2 serves as a general marker of metabolic activity for assessing host vigor and profitability across diverse insect-host interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 and C94-C98 cite prior literature and make reasonable generalizations. The comparison across systems (WCR-maize, hawkmoths-Datura, fruit flies-apples) strengthens the general hypothesis about CO2 as a metabolic activity marker. The inference is well-supported by the combination of current results and cited literature.

results.result: The impact of CO2 on WCR distribution in heterogeneous environments remains to be determined, but plant-associated CO2 is expected to contribute to uneven herbivore distribution and aggregation on plants with good nutritional status within monocultures.
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C90 acknowledge knowledge gaps and make predictions based on the experimental findings. While the prediction (C90) is reasonable given the preference data (C49-C50), it is speculative and not directly tested. Field studies in heterogeneous environments would be needed to support this prediction.

results.result: This work demonstrates how a herbivore uses CO2 perception to locate host plants, providing the first in vivo molecular manipulative validation of the model that CO2 serves as a long-distance cue while other volatiles are used at short distances. Prior studies showed root-feeding insects are attracted to CO2 in vitro, but the reliability of CO2 as a host location cue had been questioned and the distance-dependent model had not been experimentally validated.
results.evaluation: Claims C91 and C99-C104 accurately summarize the study's contribution and place it in the context of prior work. The claim of novelty (C104) regarding in vivo molecular manipulation is supported. The experimental validation of the distance-dependent model (C102-C103) is a major advance over prior correlative or in vitro studies.

results.result: WCR larvae feed almost exclusively on maize roots and cause major agricultural losses. They use multiple volatile and non-volatile chemicals for host location and discrimination. Previous studies suggested CO2 might be the only relevant volatile attractant, but larvae also respond to other volatiles when CO2 levels are similar. Putative CO2 receptors were previously identified from transcriptomic data, and ongoing efforts exist to use CO2 as bait for WCR control.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C112 provide accurate background on WCR biology, chemical ecology, and prior research. These claims cite appropriate literature and establish the rationale for the current study. This is primarily a literature review establishing context.

results.result: Carbonated water as a CO2 source creates approximately 100 ppm higher CO2 levels in olfactometer arms compared to distilled water controls.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is supported by CO2 measurements in the olfactometer system (n=4-8). This validates the experimental approach for creating CO2 gradients in behavioral assays.
